title: What's the connection between this picture and learning?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton reacts to a poster telling beginners to stop worrying about being good and simply start. He reads it as support for his Beginning-Developing-Mastering continuum, in which early skill learning looks worst precisely when it is most necessary. He argues that children should be taught from the start that being poor at something new is normal and exciting, and he warns that parents who compare children, and teachers who over-praise unfinished work, undermine this. He also criticises schools that publicise star achievers rather than star improvers. His practical answer is the rubric, which shows learners in advance what Beginning, Developing and Mastering look like, lets teachers give honest praise at the right level, and judges students against where they are rather than against a distant standard.
points: Early skill learning is the stage where performance looks worst, so learners need explicit permission to start badly and improve.
Praising outcomes rather than improvement, and publicising star achievers rather than star improvers, teaches children the wrong thing about what counts.
Rubrics that describe Beginning, Developing and Mastering let adults say Awesome and mean it, while pointing the learner toward the next good struggle.
Being a good learner means judging yourself by your current level, not against an unattempted future standard.
quotes: Early in our learning.we all need to stop worrying whether we are any ‘good’ or not. We just need to begin.
If only we could help all children and students to see that sucking at something new is a good, exciting and perfectly normal thing, even though it might not seem any of those things.

Teachers and parents who praise outcomes rather than improvements are not helping children and students learn that it is getting better - improving - that counts. The schools that give their star achievers all the publicity and not their star improvers are symbolically demonstrating to children and students what they really think counts.

Rubrics help us show children and students what steadily getting better will look like before they get there. Rubrics help us show children and students what ‘Beginning’ looks like as they engage on that perilous first step and then what ‘Developing’ and ‘Mastering’ look like as they begin to get better.

Rubrics also give us the chance to say ‘Awesome’ and mean it. When we say to a student that they have ‘produced some ‘Awesome’ work at Beginning level’, they come to learn that this congratulatory statement both gives praise and, at the same time, says ‘So…are we ready for the next good struggle?
Being a good learner is knowing that you might suck right now but that it is going to be better down the line. It’s also knowing that there is nothing wrong with this.
